title: Nothing to attain
hookLine: because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva rests in wisdom

cards: Almost everything in a modern day is built around getting somewhere. Step counts. Inbox zero.
The next level, the next degree, the next promotion. Even this app counts days, and you're on day two hundred seventy-three. Goals are good.
They get people out of bed. But when the goal becomes the whole point, the present turns into a hallway you rush through on the way to the real room.
Today the Heart Sutra says something that sounds like it would put every self-improvement book out of business: there is nothing to attain.

teach.b: Yesterday's long run of no's ended with: no wisdom and no attaining. Then the sutra draws the conclusion. Because there is nothing to attain, the bodhisattva relies on the perfection of wisdom.
The Sanskrit is aprāptitva: the state of not-getting. A strange thing to find in a text about awakening. Isn't awakening the goal?
If awakening were an object you could get, you could also grab at it, hoard it, compare yours with someone else's. That grabbing is the very craving the path is meant to loosen.
So, the sutra says, it isn't a thing you add to yourself. It's seeing clearly what was already here.
In Japan, the Zen teacher Dogen put it his own way: sitting isn't a means to awakening later; sitting is awakening, expressed now. Notice what the sutra doesn't say. It doesn't say stop practicing.
The bodhisattva still relies on wisdom, still works for the good of all beings.

teach.h: THE EFFORT STAYS, THE GRABBING GOES.
teach.b: The effort stays. What drops is the grabbing.

teach.h: A WEEK OF THE HEART SUTRA.
teach.b: Look back at the week. The shortest great sutra and its name, wisdom gone beyond. Avalokiteshvara looked deep.
Form is emptiness: nothing stands alone. Emptiness is not nothing: empty and full. Not born: no birth, no death.
No eye: hold lists lightly. And now the end of the list: nothing to get.

how: Zen communities, especially in the Soto school, often describe sitting meditation as practice without gaining ideas, and the Heart Sutra's 'nothing to attain' is chanted daily in their services.

o: a reward that comes after enough effort
not-getting: awakening isn't an object to grab
giving up on practice since it's all pointless

games.q: match each piece of this week's Heart Sutra.

s: 'nothing to attain' means Buddhists should stop practicing
the bodhisattva still relies on wisdom and works for others; what drops is the grabbing.
the line comes right after 'no wisdom and no attaining'
the sutra draws its conclusion from that list.
Dogen taught that sitting is only a means to awakening later
he taught that sitting is awakening, expressed now.

games.q: you've been meditating for months and a friend asks: so, have you got it yet? what would the Heart Sutra point to?
o: awakening isn't an object to get; the practice goes on without grabbing.
yes, and it's better than yours.
games.why: the sutra says there is nothing to attain, so the bodhisattva rests in wisdom rather than chasing a prize.

practice: For this sit, have no goal: not a calm mind, not a good session, not even a better breath.

If you catch yourself trying to do it well, smile at that and let the trying go too; if the mind wanders, that's what's happening, so that's the practice. There's nowhere this sit needs to get to; you're already here.

wordCard.voice: Aprāptitva. The state of not-getting: the Heart Sutra's reason the bodhisattva rests in wisdom instead of grasping for awakening.

orig.note: Sanskrit aprāptitva: the state of not-attaining; the Heart Sutra's reason the bodhisattva relies on the perfection of wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing to get. Awakening was never a prize to win. A week of the Heart Sutra, done.

sources.ref: Heart Sutra (Prajnaparamita-hrdaya), 'because there is nothing to attain…'
Dogen, Shobogenzo, 'Bendowa' (practice and realization are one)
